name: The City Hall Oak

location.neighbourhood: Mount Pleasant (Vancouver City Hall grounds, southwest corner)

verified_sources: https://opendata.vancouver.ca/explore/dataset/heritage-sites/ (record id 2523, heritage_register_id 2523, category LANDSCAPE RESOURCES Trees, English Oak, 453 W 12TH AV, municipaldesignationm=No)
access: Free. Stands on the public grounds of Vancouver City Hall; open daylight hours, no entry restriction.
transport: Broadway-City Hall SkyTrain (Canada Line/Millennium Line), about 8 minute walk east along W 12th Ave.
verify_notes: Vancouver Heritage Register (opendata.vancouver.ca, dataset heritage-sites) lists an English Oak at 453 W 12TH AV, heritage_register_id 2523, category LANDSCAPE RESOURCES Trees, no municipal designation bylaw. City Hall (built 1936, opened during Vancouver's golden jubilee) stands at this address; the tree is on its own grounds at the southwest corner. TWO SOURCES DISAGREE on the planting story and I am not picking a winner: (1) Nature Vancouver's own walking-tour writeup of City Hall's grounds ('Looking at Statues, Plaques, and Trees on Vancouver City Hall's Grounds') states plainly: 'In 1936, a small English oak, Quercus robur, was planted. It now fully occupies the southwest corner of the grounds' -- tying the planting to the building's 1936 opening, no royal visit mentioned. (2) Vancouver Heritage Foundation's Heritage Site Finder page for this address says 'King George, who visited in 1945, presented an oak tree that was planted on the southwest corner of the building.' This is historically suspect on its face: King George VI's only visit to BC was the May 1939 royal tour, not 1945 (he was in poor health and did not travel to Canada again after WWII); no source found corroborates a 1945 royal visit to Vancouver. I have used the 1936/building-opening dating as the basis for age_estimate because it is the more specific, internally consistent account from a dedicated naturalist-society source, but the writer should flag the royal-visit story as likely a conflation/error rather than repeat it as fact, or at minimum note both stories exist. No girth recorded anywhere; do not invent one. Location is the southwest corner of the City Hall grounds (building bounding box roughly 49.2607-49.2611 N, -123.1145 to -123.1134 W per OSM); I have placed the pin at the SW corner of that box, which is a reading of 'southwest corner of the grounds', not a taped or satellite-confirmed tree point, hence approximate. Good story potential: an oak that has 'fully occupied' its corner of a landmark civic building for 90 years, whatever the planting story's true origin.

name: The Normal School Red Oak

location.address: 555 West 12th Avenue, Vancouver, BC (City Square Shopping Centre, at the former Provincial Normal School building; register address given as 501 W 12th Ave)

verified_sources: https://opendata.vancouver.ca/explore/dataset/heritage-sites/ (record id 2522, heritage_register_id 2522, category LANDSCAPE RESOURCES Trees, Northern Red Oak, 501 W 12TH AV, municipaldesignationm=No)
access: Free. On the public plaza/grounds of City Square Shopping Centre, built around the preserved 1908-09 Provincial Normal School building. Open to the public as a commercial mall precinct.
transport: Broadway-City Hall SkyTrain station is directly adjacent (City Square Mall sits on top of/beside it).
verify_notes: ONLY ONE SOURCE FOUND for this specific tree: the Vancouver Heritage Register export (opendata.vancouver.ca, dataset heritage-sites, id 2522), which lists a Northern Red Oak at 501 W 12TH AV, category LANDSCAPE RESOURCES Trees, no municipal designation. That address is the former Provincial Normal School (built 1908-1909), designated a municipal heritage building in 1986 and adapted into City Square Shopping Centre in 1989 by Paul Merrick Architects (confirmed via heritagesitefinder.ca and the Vancouver Heritage Register policy PDF, but neither of those sources mentions the tree itself, only the building, so they corroborate the SITE, not the TREE). No independent second source naming this tree, its size or age was found in the time available. Flagging per the single-source rule rather than dropping it; a future pass could try the City of Vancouver's street-tree/park-tree GIS layers or a site visit description to raise this to two sources. Location is approximate: I geocoded City Square Shopping Centre's building footprint (49.2609, -123.1165) rather than a tree-level point, since the register carries no coordinates and I found nothing pinning the tree to a specific spot on the site.

name: The Comox Street Wingnut

location.address: 2020 Comox Street, Vancouver, BC (at Chilco Street, West End)

verified_sources: https://opendata.vancouver.ca/explore/dataset/heritage-sites/ (record id 2541, heritage_register_id 2541, category LANDSCAPE RESOURCES Trees, Caucasian Wing-Nut, 2020 COMOX ST, municipaldesignationm=No)

https://opendata.vancouver.ca/explore/dataset/public-trees/ (asset_id 69572, address '2020 COMOX ST', common_name CAUCASIAN WING NUT, genus PTEROCARYA species FRAXINIFOLIA, diameter_cm 116.8, height_m 13.7, geo_point_2d lat 49.29071399913094 lon -123.14295600005953) -- this is the City's own public/street tree inventory, a separate dataset from the Heritage Register, and it carries exact tree-level coordinates

Heritage Vancouver Society Newsletter, Volume 15 Number 2, April/May 2006, 'Out on a Limb for Heritage' by Emma Hall and Clint Robertson, https://www.heritagevancouver.org/pdf_newsletter/hvs-news-2006-02-screen.pdf (PDF fetched and read directly, not from a search summary) -- lists 'the Caucasian Wing Nut (Pterocarya fraxinifolia) located at 2020 Comox Street' under 'MUST SEE HERITAGE TREES', with a photo credited to Clint Robertson captioned 'Caucasian Wing Nut at 2020 Comox'
access: Free. Public street tree, City of Vancouver right-of-way at the Comox/Chilco corner in the West End.
transport: About a 10 minute walk from Burrard/Robson downtown, or the #5 or #6 bus along Denman/Davie to the West End.
verify_notes: Three independent sources agree on species and location: the Heritage Register (id 2541, no municipal bylaw designation), the City's separate public-trees street inventory (asset_id 69572, which is how I got real tree-level coordinates and a real diameter, since the Register itself carries none), and a 2006 Heritage Vancouver Society newsletter that named it one of the city's 'must see' heritage trees with its own photograph. diameter_cm 116.8 from the city's own measurement converts to a girth of about 367 cm (116.8 x pi). This is the largest Caucasian wingnut of 43 wingnuts (both this species and the related Chinese wingnut) recorded anywhere in Vancouver's public-trees dataset, next largest being 111.8 cm diameter at 6875 Yew St. A widely repeated web claim (seen only in search-engine AI summaries, never on a page I could fetch and read directly, so NOT used as a sourced fact per the 'search summary is a lead, not a source' rule) says the tree is 'over a hundred years old' and that its crown 'spreads from one side of the street to the other'. I have used 'over a century' as a vague, unsourced-but-plausible age band given the exceptional 116.8 cm trunk diameter (this genus grows fast, so this is a wide, honest band rather than a precise figure) and NOT claimed the street-spanning crown detail, which the writer should treat as unconfirmed colour rather than fact unless a future pass finds it on a page directly. The public-trees asset_id 242964 at the same street address (an Eastern Redbud, planted 2012) is a different, unrelated tree and not part of this entry.

name: The Planetarium Magnolias

location.address: H.R. MacMillan Space Centre, 1100 Chestnut Street, Vanier Park, Vancouver, BC

verified_sources: https://opendata.vancouver.ca/explore/dataset/heritage-sites/ (record id 2540, heritage_register_id 2540, category LANDSCAPE RESOURCES Trees, Saucer Magnolia, 1100 CHESTNUT ST, municipaldesignationm=No)

Heritage Vancouver Society Newsletter, Volume 15 Number 2, April/May 2006, 'Out on a Limb for Heritage', https://www.heritagevancouver.org/pdf_newsletter/hvs-news-2006-02-screen.pdf (PDF fetched and read directly): 'two Soulange Magnolias (Magnolia x soulangiana). Planted in 1912 outside the then newly built Court House (now the VAG) they were slated for disposal in 1966 to make room for the new provincial government fountain. The Public outcry was such that landscape contractor K. Johnsen could not destroy the trees and instead transported them to his own property. In 1968 the Vancouver Park Board acquired the trees and moved them to their present home, flanking the ramp entrances to the H.R. MacMillan Planetarium.'
access: Free to view from outside (grounds of the Museum of Vancouver / H.R. MacMillan Space Centre in Vanier Park, a public park); the Space Centre building itself charges admission but the ramp and its flanking trees are on open museum-forecourt grounds.
transport: Vanier Park, about a 15 minute walk from Granville Island or across the Burrard Bridge from downtown; bus #2 or #22 to Cornwall/Cypress.
verify_notes: TWO trees folded into one entry, per the register-twins rule: the Heritage Register lists a single 'Saucer Magnolia' entry (id 2540) at 1100 Chestnut St, but the only real narrative source describes a PAIR planted together and moved together, flanking the two ramp entrances to the H.R. MacMillan Planetarium (now the H.R. MacMillan Space Centre, part of the Museum of Vancouver complex in Vanier Park). Documented planting date: 1912, originally outside the old Vancouver Court House (now the Vancouver Art Gallery downtown, several km away). Rescued from destruction by public outcry in 1966 when the province wanted the site for a fountain; a landscape contractor kept them on his own property for two years; the Vancouver Park Board acquired and replanted them at their current Vanier Park site in 1968. Age is a DERIVED estimate from the documented 1912 planting date (about 114 years as of 2026), broadened slightly (108-118) to allow for transplant stress/uncertainty in exact planting month. This is the only source found beyond the bare register line; a second, fully independent confirmation (a photo, a Park Board record, a news clipping of the 1966 controversy) would strengthen this further, but I did not find one in the time available, so this is not flagged only because the newsletter account is detailed, specific and internally consistent (named contractor, named institutions, two clear dates) rather than a bare mention. Location is the museum/planetarium forecourt in Vanier Park; I geocoded the H.R. MacMillan Space Centre building (a public landmark) rather than a tree-level point, hence approximate.
